catalog_quote: How should long vowels be interpreted phonologically? This may be seen as vowel length as it is, or as the phonetic manifestation of the stress (or accent) system as in the case of other Philippine languages (see Zorc 1993). Nevertheless, the present study demonstrates that it is phonologically the length of a vowel, rather than the phonetic manifestation of the stress system in two respects. First, if the long vowel is really a manifestation of lexical stress, the place of the stress may shift by affixation as in English ... However, this kind of shift is not observed in Arta, as shown below: (45) pe:nas > pe:nas-an, (not pena:s-an) 'wipe' ... The second defining feature is that each word (not a root) has one stress nucleus. Even if two stresses are observed within a single word, they have a phonetic asymmetry to the extent that one stress is considered to be primary, the other secondary (e.g. dòcuméntary, téxt-bòok). This is not the case in Arta. Several words do have more than one long vowel without such phonetic asymmetry. ... Since none of these two facts favour the long-vowel-as-stress analysis, this contrast will be treated more appropriately as the phonological long-short distinction of vowels. [p. 86 fn. 1] This does not work in Arta since the language has no stress system (See §2.1.3). [p. 83] Although accentual system seen in some other Philippine languages has lost in Arta, the language developed short-long contrast of vowels through compensatory lengthening and vowel fusion.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arta has no word stress/accent system. What looks like the penultimate 'accent' of other Philippine languages is phonemic vowel length (bi:lèg 'bracelet' vs bilèg 'fastness'; ana: 'child' vs a:na: 'children'): length is fixed to the root and never shifts under affixation (pe:nas > pe:nas-an, not pena:s-an), and a word may carry several long vowels with no primary/secondary asymmetry (ta:ta:me:ta, pe:be:bu:d=u). The inherited Proto-Philippine accent contrast was lost; Arta's long vowels arose independently by compensatory lengthening and vowel fusion, and stress in loanwords is reinterpreted as length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: the source argues explicitly that words with more than one long vowel show no primary/secondary prominence asymmetry (p. 52), which is one of its two reasons for rejecting a stress analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: Only an intonational, phrase-level phenomenon: at a clause boundary or utterance end speakers 'may stress the vowel of the final syllable by gaining its loudness and/or making it longer' (p. 42, 'emphatic stress', e.g. [dɔn.na.ba.gát]); this is not lexical word stress. Loanwords from Ilokano, Yogad, Spanish and English have their source stress reinterpreted as a long vowel; /e/ and /o/ are always long (pp. 51, 60-61).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (roots and affixed words, with citation and text forms); the only prominence described at phrase level is the final-syllable emphatic intonation. Author's field site: Nagtipunan, Quirino Province; ~10 native speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: Arta (glottocode arta1239, ISO atz), also called Edilod by its speakers per Kimoto's later titles; Kimoto's description is of the Arta of Nagtipunan, Quirino Province (about 10 native speakers, living among Casiguran Agta communities). Reid 1989 is based on a short 1987 elicitation and describes the same language. No separate dialects are distinguished in any source seen.

new_statements.quote: Syllables appear to have a quantity-sensitive constraint: a long vowel + consonant, or diphthong (short vowel + glide) + consonant is rarely found. This syllabic pattern is best understood in terms of a mora constraint that a syllable should be composed of one or two mora. All of the vocabulary items excluding kabba:t 'like, want' and manga:sa:sbiw 'yawn' have a legitimate syllable structure in terms of this constraint. The accent system remains unclear, but it appears that there is no clear pitch or stress accent in Arta.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The author finds no clear pitch accent or stress accent in Arta; the accent system is left as unclear. Vowel length is phonemic (bilag 'speed' vs. bi:lag 'necklace', §2.1, p. 86) and is treated as segmental length, not as the reflex of a stress system. No stress placement is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. The only exceptions noted are to the one-or-two-mora syllable constraint (kabba:t 'like, want', manga:sa:sbiw 'yawn').
new_statements.identity_note: The 2014 paper describes the Arta spoken in the Municipality of Nagtipunan, Quirino Province (Barangays Disimungal, San Ramos, Pongo, Sangbay; communities at Purok Kalbo, Pulang Lupa, Tilitilan), from 13 months of fieldwork in 2012-13 with ~1000 vocabulary items; no dialect split is named.
